lesson.title: From DNA to RNA: An Introduction to Transcription
lesson.summary: Transcription is the process of copying the DNA sequence of a gene into a complementary RNA molecule, the first step a cell takes in reading out its genetic instructions.
lesson.body:
DNA replication, covered throughout the earlier chapters of this unit, copies an entire genome so it can be passed on to new cells. Transcription is a different kind of copying: instead of duplicating all of the DNA, it copies just one gene at a time into a molecule of RNA, which the cell can then use more directly. Recall that RNA, like DNA, is a nucleic acid built from nucleotides, but it is normally single stranded, uses the sugar ribose rather than deoxyribose, and uses the base uracil (U) in place of thymine (T).

Because DNA is a double helix of two complementary strands, only one of those two strands, called the template strand, is actually read and copied for a given gene. An enzyme (RNA polymerase, the subject of the next chapter) locally unwinds a short stretch of the double helix at the gene, exposing the template strand, and then builds a new RNA molecule using the same base pairing rules that govern DNA, with one adjustment: since RNA uses uracil instead of thymine, a template adenine (A) pairs with uracil (U) in the new RNA strand, while a template thymine (T) still pairs with adenine (A) in the RNA. Guanine and cytosine pair with each other exactly as they do in DNA.

For example, if a gene's template strand reads 3'-TACGGATC-5', the RNA transcript synthesized from it will read 5'-AUGCCUAG-3', matching the template base for base, but with U taking the place T would occupy in a DNA copy. Just as with DNA polymerase, the enzyme reads the template strand in the 3' to 5' direction and builds the new RNA strand 5' to 3'.

The other DNA strand, the one not used as a template, is called the coding or sense strand, because its sequence matches the RNA transcript almost exactly (again, except that it has T where the RNA has U). This is a useful shortcut for reading gene sequences directly off of DNA databases without having to mentally flip and complement anything.

The RNA molecule produced by transcription can serve several roles depending on the gene, but the most common outcome, and the focus of the rest of this unit, is messenger RNA (mRNA): a transcript that carries the instructions for building a protein. In eukaryotic cells, this transcript is not immediately ready for use. It must first be processed, a topic covered in the mRNA Processing chapter, before it leaves the nucleus to be translated. The chapters that follow examine the machinery of transcription in more detail: the enzyme that does the copying (RNA polymerase), the sequences that tell it where to start (promoter regions), the signals that tell it where to stop (transcription termination), and the finishing touches applied to the transcript before it is ready for use.
